tang-dynasty.name: Tang dynasty
tang-dynasty.summary: Chinese imperial dynasty that ruled from 618 to 907, with an interruption from 690 to 705, widely regarded as a golden age of cosmopolitan Chinese civilisation.

cold-food-festival.name: Cold Food Festival
cold-food-festival.summary: A traditional Chinese holiday that began with mourning the nobleman Jie Zitui in the 7th century BC and, by the Tang dynasty, grew into an East Asian occasion for venerating ancestors.

three-kingdoms.name: Three Kingdoms period
three-kingdoms.summary: A period from 220 to 280 CE when China was split among the states of Cao Wei, Shu Han and Eastern Wu after the Han dynasty's collapse, marked by plague, famine and civil war.

qingming-festival.name: Qingming Festival
qingming-festival.summary: Traditional Chinese spring festival, also called Tomb-Sweeping Day, when families visit and clean ancestors' graves and make ritual offerings.

bing-bread.name: Bing
bing-bread.summary: A wheat-flour-based Chinese bread with a flattened, disk-like shape, resembling the flatbreads, pancakes, and crêpes of other cuisines.

qimin-yaoshu.name: Qimin Yaoshu
qimin-yaoshu.summary: The best-preserved ancient Chinese agricultural text, written around 544 CE by the official Jia Sixie, covering farming, food storage, brewing and cooking.

mogao-caves.name: Mogao Caves
mogao-caves.summary: A system of about 500 Buddhist temple caves near Dunhuang, China, first dug in 366 CE and holding some of the finest Buddhist art made over 1,000 years; a hidden manuscript library was found there in 1900.

dunhuang.name: Dunhuang
dunhuang.summary: Oasis city in northwestern China and major Silk Road stop, known for the nearby Mogao Caves and its position at the entrance to the Hexi Corridor.

northern-wei.name: Northern Wei
northern-wei.summary: Imperial Chinese dynasty ruled by the Tuoba clan of the Xianbei, ruling northern China from 386 to 535 AD; noted for unifying northern China in 439 and firmly establishing Buddhism.

chang-an.name: Chang'an
chang-an.summary: Capital of several Chinese dynasties, including the Western Han and Tang, from 202 BCE to 907 CE, and at times the largest city in the world; known today as Xi'an.

cai-lun.name: Cai Lun
cai-lun.summary: A Chinese court official of the Eastern Han dynasty traditionally credited with improving papermaking by adding pulp from bark and hemp.

han-dynasty.name: Han dynasty
han-dynasty.summary: An imperial Chinese dynasty (202 BC–220 AD) seen as a golden age of Chinese history; the majority Chinese ethnic group, language and script are named after it.

song-dynasty.name: Song dynasty
song-dynasty.summary: Imperial Chinese dynasty that ruled from 960 to 1279, later split into a northern and southern period after losing northern China to the Jurchen Jin dynasty, before its conquest by the Mongols.

ming-dynasty.name: Ming dynasty
ming-dynasty.summary: China's last dynasty ruled by the Han majority, reigning 1368 to 1644 after the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty's fall, founded by the Hongwu Emperor.

battle-of-talas.name: Battle of Talas
battle-of-talas.summary: A 751 battle in which the Abbasid Caliphate and its Karluk allies defeated the Tang dynasty's army for control of Central Asia, ending Tang westward expansion; Chinese prisoners taken there are said to have introduced papermaking to West Asia.

wang-xuance.name: Wang Xuance
wang-xuance.summary: Chinese diplomat, military general and travel writer active in the 7th century.

arunasva.name: Arunasva
arunasva.summary: Governor of Tirabhukti in modern north Bihar who seized the throne of Kannauj after King Harsha's death and repelled an Arab invasion.

kannauj.name: Kannauj
kannauj.summary: An ancient city in Uttar Pradesh, India, once capital of several kingdoms and long fought over by rival empires for control of the Gangetic Plains.

songtsen-gampo.name: Songtsen Gampo
songtsen-gampo.summary: The 33rd king of Tibet, ruling from around 618 to 650, who founded the Tibetan Empire, introduced Buddhism and unified the Tibetan Plateau.

narendradeva.name: Narendradeva
narendradeva.summary: A Licchavi king of Nepal who reigned from 643 to 679, opened diplomatic ties with China and helped make Nepal a prosperous trade gateway between India and Tibet.

talas-river.name: Talas River
talas-river.summary: A river rising in Kyrgyzstan and flowing into Kazakhstan, 661 kilometres long, near which Tang and Abbasid forces clashed in 751.

syr-darya.name: Syr Darya
syr-darya.summary: A 2,256-kilometre river in Central Asia, historically called the Jaxartes, flowing from Kyrgyzstan through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan toward the Aral Sea.

gao-xianzhi.name: Gao Xianzhi
gao-xianzhi.summary: A Tang dynasty general of Goguryeo descent who led campaigns into Central Asia and commanded the Tang army at its 751 defeat at the Battle of Talas; executed in 756 on a corruption charge.

transoxiana.name: Transoxiana
transoxiana.summary: A Central Asian region beyond the Amu Darya river, named by Alexander the Great's troops in the 4th century BCE and later a Persian Achaemenid province called Sogdia.

harsha.name: Harsha
harsha.summary: Emperor of Kannauj from 606 to 647 who expanded his realm across much of northern India and hosted the Chinese traveller Xuanzang, who praised his justice and generosity.

tibetan-empire.name: Tibetan Empire
tibetan-empire.summary: An empire centered on the Tibetan Plateau, formed in the 7th century under Songtsen Gampo and later stretching from China to Afghanistan and India.

licchavis-of-nepal.name: Licchavis
licchavis-of-nepal.summary: A dynasty that ruled a kingdom in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley from about 400 to 879 CE, originating from the Licchavis of Vaishali in what is now Bihar, India.

princess-wencheng.name: Princess Wencheng
princess-wencheng.summary: A member of the Tang dynasty's imperial clan who married Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo in 641, sealing a marriage alliance between Tang China and Tibet.

hindu-kush.name: Hindu Kush
hindu-kush.summary: An 800-kilometre mountain range running from Afghanistan into Pakistan and Tajikistan, historically a center of Buddhism and a crossing point between Central and South Asia.

pamir-mountains.name: Pamir Mountains
pamir-mountains.summary: A mountain range in Central and South Asia where the Tian Shan, Karakoram, Kunlun, Hindu Kush and Himalayas meet, known since Victorian times as the 'Roof of the World.'

harun-al-rashid.name: Harun al-Rashid
harun-al-rashid.summary: Fifth Abbasid caliph, reigning 786 to 809, whose rule is traditionally seen as the start of the Islamic Golden Age; he founded the House of Wisdom library in Baghdad.

emperor-taizong-of-tang.name: Emperor Taizong of Tang
emperor-taizong-of-tang.summary: Second emperor of China's Tang dynasty (598–649), regarded as one of China's greatest rulers; his reign, the Zhenguan era, is considered a golden age of Chinese history.

battle-of-chabuheluo.name: Battle of Chabuheluo
battle-of-chabuheluo.summary: A 648 battle fought between an alliance led by the Tang dynasty and the Kingdom of Kannauj.

gandaki-river.name: Gandaki River
gandaki-river.summary: A major river in Nepal and tributary of the Ganges, known for its deep Himalayan canyon and called Kali Gandaki in its upper reaches.

kucha.name: Kucha
kucha.summary: Ancient Tocharian Buddhist kingdom on the Silk Road in the Tarim Basin, now the site of Kuqa town in Xinjiang, China.

aksu-city.name: Aksu City
aksu-city.summary: A city in Xinjiang, China, at the northern edge of the Tarim Basin, whose name means 'white water'; historically an oasis town with a mainly cotton-based agricultural economy.

tarim-basin.name: Tarim Basin
tarim-basin.summary: A large endorheic basin in Xinjiang, northwestern China, dominated by the Taklamakan Desert and historically called Altishahr.

fergana-valley.name: Fergana Valley
fergana-valley.summary: Fertile Central Asian valley spanning parts of modern Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, a historic crossroads of Greek, Chinese, Bactrian and Parthian civilizations and homeland of Mughal founder Babur.

classical-chinese.name: Literary Chinese
classical-chinese.summary: The written literary form of Chinese used from the 5th century BCE and adopted across Vietnam, Korea, Japan and the Ryukyus as a shared language of scholarship and administration until the early 20th century.

xuanzang.name: Xuanzang
xuanzang.summary: 7th-century Chinese Buddhist monk and traveler (602–664) whose journey to India in 629–645 brought hundreds of Buddhist texts back to China for translation.

records-of-the-western-regions.name: Great Tang Records on the Western Regions
records-of-the-western-regions.summary: An account of the Buddhist monk Xuanzang's 19-year journey to India and back, compiled in 646 from his dictation by his disciple Bianji, describing the people and places along his route.

miscellaneous-morsels-from-youyang.name: Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang
miscellaneous-morsels-from-youyang.summary: A 9th-century Tang dynasty book by Duan Chengshi collecting legends, anecdotes and miscellany, including an early version of the Cinderella story.

taiping-guangji.name: Taiping Guangji
taiping-guangji.summary: A collection of over 7,000 stories compiled in 978 under the Song dynasty, preserving many earlier tales—including famous Tang dynasty stories—that would otherwise have been lost.

chuanqi-short-story-and-novella.name: Chuanqi
chuanqi-short-story-and-novella.summary: A form of Classical Chinese short story or novella that began in the Tang dynasty, covering themes of love, gods and demons, knights-errant, and history.

classic-of-poetry.name: Classic of Poetry
classic-of-poetry.summary: The oldest surviving collection of Chinese poetry, comprising 305 works from the 11th to 7th centuries BC and traditionally said to be edited by Confucius.

zheng-xuan.name: Zheng Xuan
zheng-xuan.summary: Chinese philosopher, politician and writer (127–200) at the end of the Eastern Han dynasty, a student of Ma Rong known for his scholarly annotated editions of classical texts.

li-bai.name: Li Bai
li-bai.summary: Chinese poet (c. 701-762) of the Tang dynasty, regarded as one of the greatest in Chinese history, celebrated for poems on friendship, nature and drinking, with around 1,000 surviving works.

mount-taibai.name: Mount Taibai
mount-taibai.summary: The tallest mountain in Shaanxi Province, China, and the subject of a poem by the Tang poet Li Bo.

du-fu.name: Du Fu
du-fu.summary: A Tang dynasty poet and official (712–770) whose nearly 1,500 surviving poems, shaped by displacement during the An Lushan rebellion, earned him the title "Poet-Historian".

an-lushan-rebellion.name: An Lushan rebellion
an-lushan-rebellion.summary: A civil war in Tang dynasty China from 755 to 763 that briefly overthrew the government, causing massive depopulation and marking a major turning point in medieval Chinese history.

sangluan.name: Sangluan
sangluan.summary: A genre of Classical Chinese poetry from the Yuan dynasty era, focused on the devastation, death and destruction caused by war.

wenyuan-yinghua.name: Wenyuan Yinghua
wenyuan-yinghua.summary: A 10th-century Chinese anthology of poetry, odes, songs and writings compiled under imperial order between 982 and 986, one of the Four Great Books of Song.

book-of-sui.name: Book of Sui
book-of-sui.summary: The official history of China's Sui dynasty (581–618), completed in 636 by Wei Zheng and others and considered a primary source.

you-ming-lu.name: You Ming Lu
you-ming-lu.summary: A 5th-century Chinese collection of supernatural tales, one of the earliest to show Buddhist influence, reconstructed after being lost before the Song dynasty.

shen-yue.name: Shen Yue
shen-yue.summary: Chinese historian, poet and politician (441–513) who served three southern dynasties and wrote the Book of Song, a history of the earlier Liu Song dynasty.

lu-xun.name: Lu Xun
lu-xun.summary: Chinese writer (1881–1936), pen name of Zhou Shuren, a leading figure of modern Chinese literature known for pioneering vernacular fiction and sharp, satirical essays.

sun-simiao.name: Sun Simiao
sun-simiao.summary: A Chinese physician and writer of the Sui and Tang dynasties (581–682 CE), honored as China's 'King of Medicine' for his major contributions to Chinese medicine.

li-chunfeng.name: Li Chunfeng
li-chunfeng.summary: Chinese astronomer, mathematician and historian (602-670) of the early Tang dynasty who directed the Imperial Astronomical Bureau, reformed the calendar, and annotated the classical Chinese mathematical canon.

yi-xing.name: Yi Xing
yi-xing.summary: An eighth-century Tang dynasty Buddhist monk, astronomer and calendar reformer who built a celestial globe with a liquid-driven escapement, the first in a long line of Chinese astronomical clocks.

diamond-sutra.name: Diamond Sutra
diamond-sutra.summary: A Mahayana Buddhist sutra especially influential in East Asia and Zen Buddhism; a Tang-dynasty copy dated 868 CE, found at Dunhuang, is considered the oldest surviving printed book.

dunhuang-manuscripts.name: Dunhuang manuscripts
dunhuang-manuscripts.summary: Collection of handwritten and printed texts in Chinese, Tibetan and other languages, discovered in 1900 in a sealed cave near Dunhuang and later sold to European scholars.

armillary-sphere.name: Armillary sphere
armillary-sphere.summary: Model of the celestial sphere made of rings representing lines such as the ecliptic, invented separately in ancient China and Greece and later used in the Islamic world and medieval Europe.

ten-computational-canons.name: Ten Mathematical Manuals
ten-computational-canons.summary: A collection of ten Chinese mathematical texts spanning pre-Han to early Tang times, compiled in the 650s as the official curriculum for imperial mathematics examinations.

emperor-wen-of-sui.name: Emperor Wen of Sui
emperor-wen-of-sui.summary: Founding emperor of China's Sui dynasty (541–604), a Buddhist ruler who reunified China in 589 after nearly three centuries of division and began the Grand Canal.

northern-zhou.name: Northern Zhou
northern-zhou.summary: Xianbei-led Chinese dynasty founded by the Yuwen clan, lasting from 557 to 581 AD, succeeding the Western Wei dynasty and overthrown by the Sui dynasty.

emperor-taizu-of-song.name: Emperor Taizu of Song
emperor-taizu-of-song.summary: Founding emperor of China's Song dynasty (927–976), a general who seized the throne in a coup and went on to reunify most of China proper.

later-zhou.name: Later Zhou
later-zhou.summary: The last of China's Five Dynasties, ruling most of northern China until succeeded by the Northern Song dynasty in 960.

five-dynasties-and-ten-kingdoms-period.name: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period
five-dynasties-and-ten-kingdoms-period.summary: An era of political division in China from 907 to 979 CE, with five dynasties succeeding each other in the north while over a dozen states, chiefly ten kingdoms, ruled the south.
five-dynasties-and-ten-kingdoms-period.source_title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period

three-departments-and-six-ministries.name: Three Departments and Six Ministries
three-departments-and-six-ministries.summary: The main government structure of imperial China from the Sui to Yuan dynasties, splitting administration into three top departments and six ministries handling specific state functions.

imperial-examination.name: Imperial examination
imperial-examination.summary: Merit-based system for selecting Chinese state officials, formalized under the Tang and Song dynasties and lasting until its abolition in 1905.

fubing-system.name: Fubing system
fubing-system.summary: A local militia system used in Imperial China from the 6th to 8th centuries, starting under the Western Wei and later adopted by the Sui and Tang dynasties.

equal-field-system.name: Equal-field system
equal-field-system.summary: A Chinese system of land ownership and distribution used from the Northern Wei dynasty, from about 485 AD, to the mid-Tang dynasty, meant to curb aristocratic land control and support small farmers.

grand-canal-china.name: Grand Canal
grand-canal-china.summary: The world's longest artificial waterway, linking rivers and lakes across North and East China to move goods between the north and south for centuries.

luoyang.name: Luoyang
luoyang.summary: A city in Henan province, China, among the oldest in the country and the earliest of its Four Great Ancient Capitals, at the meeting of the Luo and Yellow rivers.

goguryeo-sui-war.name: Goguryeo–Sui War
goguryeo-sui-war.summary: Series of invasions (598–614 AD) by China's Sui dynasty against the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo; the Sui's defeat was a pivotal cause of the dynasty's fall.

goguryeo.name: Goguryeo
goguryeo.summary: Korean kingdom (37 BC–668 AD) covering much of the Korean peninsula and parts of Manchuria, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea and the source of the name Korea.

kaifeng.name: Kaifeng
kaifeng.summary: City in Henan, China, formerly called Bianjing, that served as capital of the Northern Song dynasty until it was sacked in 1127.

sui-dynasty.name: Sui dynasty
sui-dynasty.summary: Chinese imperial dynasty that ruled from 581 to 618 CE, reuniting China after centuries of division and laying groundwork for the following Tang dynasty's golden age.

zoroastrianism.name: Zoroastrianism
zoroastrianism.summary: An ancient Iranian religion founded on the teachings of Zoroaster, centred on the deity Ahura Mazda and the choice between truth and chaos, once Greater Iran's dominant faith under the Sassanid Empire.

church-of-the-east.name: Church of the East
church-of-the-east.summary: An Eastern Christian branch, also called the Nestorian Church, that arose from 5th-century Christological disputes and originated in Mesopotamia under the Parthian Empire.

manichaeism.name: Manichaeism
manichaeism.summary: A major dualistic religion founded in the 3rd century CE by the prophet Mani, teaching a cosmic struggle between light and darkness and drawing on Zoroastrian, Christian and Buddhist traditions.

six-dynasties.name: Six Dynasties
six-dynasties.summary: A collective term for six Han-ruled Chinese dynasties from the early 3rd to late 6th century AD, between the Eastern Han and the Sui dynasty.

chen-dynasty.name: Chen dynasty
chen-dynasty.summary: The last of China's Southern dynasties (557 to 589 CE), founded by Chen Baxian; it strengthened southern China's economy and culture before being conquered by the Sui dynasty.

wang-tong-philosopher.name: Wang Tong
wang-tong-philosopher.summary: Chinese philosopher and politician of the Sui dynasty who lived from 584 to 617.

alopen.name: Alopen
alopen.summary: First recorded Christian missionary to reach China, arriving in the Tang capital Chang'an in 635 and gaining acceptance from Emperor Taizong.

fang-xuanling.name: Fang Xuanling
fang-xuanling.summary: Tang dynasty statesman and writer (579–648) who served as chancellor under Emperor Taizong and led the editing of the historical record Book of Jin.

zhiyi.name: Zhiyi
zhiyi.summary: A Chinese Buddhist monk and philosopher (538–597 CE) considered the founder of the Tiantai Buddhist tradition, who built a system of thought centered on the Lotus Sutra.

tiantai.name: Tiantai
tiantai.summary: An East Asian school of Mahayana Buddhism that developed in 6th-century China, centered on the Lotus Sutra and chiefly founded by Zhiyi.

mohe-zhiguan.name: Mohe Zhiguan
mohe-zhiguan.summary: A major Buddhist doctrinal work based on lectures given in 594 by the Chinese Tiantai patriarch Zhiyi, later compiled by his disciple Guanding; central to Tiantai and Japanese Tendai Buddhism.

lotus-sutra.name: Lotus Sutra
lotus-sutra.summary: One of the most influential Mahāyāna Buddhist scriptures, teaching that all Buddhist paths lead to Buddhahood; it founded the Tiantai school and later Tendai and Nichiren traditions.

ashoka.name: Ashoka
ashoka.summary: Emperor of the Mauryan dynasty from about 268 BCE, whose empire covered much of the Indian subcontinent; after conquering Kalinga he turned to promoting Buddhism across Asia.

maurya-empire.name: Maurya Empire
maurya-empire.summary: A large Iron Age empire in South Asia founded around 320 BCE by Chandragupta Maurya and lasting until 185 BCE, reaching its height under his grandson Ashoka.

shangqing-school.name: Shangqing School
shangqing-school.summary: A Daoist movement begun in the Western Jin dynasty that favored meditation, visualization and breathing over alchemy, becoming the dominant school of Daoism during the Tang dynasty.

emperor-yang-of-sui.name: Emperor Yang of Sui
emperor-yang-of-sui.summary: Second emperor of the Sui dynasty (604–618), known for completing the Grand Canal and rebuilding the Great Wall, but whose costly wars and construction projects bankrupted the empire and sparked revolt.

emperor-wuzong-of-tang.name: Emperor Wuzong of Tang
emperor-wuzong-of-tang.summary: Tang dynasty emperor who reigned from 840 to 846, chiefly remembered for the religious persecution of Buddhism during his rule, though also known for repelling Uyghur incursions and trusting chancellor Li Deyu.

adam-monk.name: Jingjing
adam-monk.summary: 8th-century Syriac Christian monk and scholar in China who wrote the text on the Nestorian Stele, recording the Church of the East's history there from 635 to 781.

saich.name: Saichō
saich.summary: A Japanese Buddhist monk (767-822) who founded the Tendai school after studying in Tang China in 804, establishing its headquarters at Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei near Kyoto.

mount-hiei.name: Mount Hiei
mount-hiei.summary: Mountain near Kyoto, Japan, site of the Enryaku-ji temple founded in 788 that became the center of the Tendai Buddhist sect.

mount-tai.name: Mount Tai
mount-tai.summary: Sacred mountain in Shandong, China, the foremost of the country's five Sacred Mountains and a ceremonial site for over 3,000 years.

k-kai.name: Kūkai
k-kai.summary: A Japanese Buddhist monk, calligrapher and poet (774–835) who studied esoteric Buddhism in China and founded Japan's Shingon school on his return.

ximing-temple.name: Ximing Temple
ximing-temple.summary: A renowned Buddhist temple in Chang'an (Xi'an), established in 656, famed for its library and as a center where monks including Xuanzang translated Indian scriptures.

chan-buddhism.name: Chan Buddhism
chan-buddhism.summary: A Mahāyāna Chinese Buddhist tradition that developed from the 6th century CE, flourished under the Tang and Song, and spread abroad as Zen in Japan and Seon in Korea.

nestorianism.name: Nestorianism
nestorianism.summary: A set of Christian theological teachings on the two natures or persons of Christ, originally tied to bishop Nestorius and condemned at the Council of Ephesus.

emperor-xuanzong-of-tang.name: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang
emperor-xuanzong-of-tang.summary: Tang dynasty emperor whose 44-year reign, the longest of the dynasty, began with a golden age but ended in sharp decline after the An Lushan rebellion.

mani-prophet.name: Mani
mani-prophet.summary: An Iranian prophet (c. 216–274 CE) who founded Manichaeism, born near Ctesiphon in the Parthian Empire and later imprisoned and killed under the Sasanian ruler Bahram I.

laozi.name: Laozi
laozi.summary: Traditional name for an ancient Chinese philosopher credited as author of the Tao Te Ching and founder of Taoism, said to have lived in the 6th century BC, though his historical existence is debated.

huahujing.name: Huahujing
huahujing.summary: A Taoist text traditionally attributed to Laozi, surviving only through quotations in a manuscript found at the Mogao Caves in Dunhuang.
